glucose
islet

HIGH glucose · solid red → beta cells release insulin; liver stores glucose as glycogen and makes less; muscle and fat bring GLUT4 to the surface and take glucose up; blood glucose falls.

LOW glucose · dashed blue → alpha cells release glucagon; the liver breaks down glycogen and makes glucose; blood glucose rises.

somatostatin ⊣ violet, blunt end delta cells hold back both beta and alpha cells. The tonic brake was shown in mouse islets (Hauge-Evans 2009) and secretion rises modestly with glucose (Rorsman and Huising 2018).

Sources, wording and limits

Educational only, not medical advice. Schematic, not to scale (cells in panel B are not to scale either). Hormone levels come from a small qualitative model, not measurements. The figure shows no measured values. Hormone and transporter levels are drawn from a small qualitative model; the only numbers are the published cell proportions below.

  • Islet architecture and proportions. Cabrera et al., PNAS 2006 (PMID 16461897). Human islets: insulin cells 48-59 %, glucagon cells 33-46 %, somatostatin cells 8-12 % of the islet, depending on pancreatic region (n = 5 donors); the three types are mostly intermixed and the arrangement varies. Mouse islets: insulin cells clustered in the core, glucagon and somatostatin cells in the mantle; the paper's text gives more than 70 % beta and fewer than 20 % alpha for mouse-like islets. The mouse core-mantle layout and its proportions are schematic (its Fig 1F bars are not reproduced). The drawing has 27 cells: human 14 beta, 10 alpha, 3 delta (52 / 37 / 11 %); mouse 20 beta, 5 alpha, 2 delta (74 / 19 / 7 %). Cell counts are a schematic sample, not a real islet. The capillaries are one schematic layout used for both species.
  • Islet blood flow (rodent). Samols et al., J Clin Invest 1988 (PMID 2455737): in the perfused rat pancreas, functional data suggest perfusion runs from the beta-cell core outward to the mantle.
  • Hormone actions and targets. Röder et al., Exp Mol Med 2016 (PMID 26964835): insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose; liver, muscle and fat as targets.
  • GLUT4 translocation. Bryant, Govers and James, Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 2002 (PMID 11994746): in muscle and fat, insulin stimulates delivery of GLUT4 from an intracellular location to the cell surface. Huang and Czech, Cell Metab 2007 (PMID 17403369): GLUT4 is the principal insulin-responsive transporter in skeletal muscle. The abstracts do not name the intermediate signalling steps, so the figure says "insulin-receptor signalling (not drawn)".
  • Liver glucose transporter. Thorens, Diabetologia 2015 (PMID 25421524): GLUT2 is expressed in liver. It also notes a glucose output route that may not depend on GLUT2 alone, so the output arrow leaves the cell without a transporter.
  • Somatostatin. Hauge-Evans et al., Diabetes 2009 (PMID 18984743): in Sst knockout mice, islet insulin and glucagon secretion were enhanced, indicating a tonic inhibitory influence of delta-cell somatostatin (mouse evidence). Rorsman and Huising, Nat Rev Endocrinol 2018 (PMID 29773871): delta-cell KATP channels close at elevated glucose, increasing somatostatin secretion. The rise drawn here is a modest, qualitative one.

Notes on species and GLUT4. Beta about 60 % at the centre with alpha about 30 % at the edge mixes two species. Cabrera et al. report about 60 % beta and 30 % alpha for human islets, which lack a beta core and alpha rim; the core-and-mantle layout belongs to the mouse, where beta cells exceed 70 %. The toggle therefore shows each species with its own layout and proportions. GLUT4 is drawn only in muscle and fat; the liver shows glycogen, glucose output and GLUT2 instead. Red with solid lines marks the high-glucose pathway and blue with dashed lines the low-glucose pathway, so colour is never the only cue.

Simplified. One islet of about thirty cells stands for thousands. The vessel loop is in series, where real circulation is parallel, and blood from the islets reaches the liver first through the portal vein. Cells in panel B are not to scale (adipocytes are much larger than hepatocytes). The loop's set point, time constants and slopes are invented to show the shape of negative feedback (a rise settles back, a fall settles back) and carry no units. Omitted: PP cells, nerves, incretins, other hormones, insulin-receptor signalling steps, and adrenaline. Somatostatin rises modestly with glucose in the model; the tonic-inhibition evidence is from mouse islets and the human evidence is not drawn.
